name: Cleveland 'Cleve' Marchbanks
languages: Spanish (from the Westside garages, where he learned his trade)
equipment: Leather jacket, brown horsehide, over a cabbie's cap and a sweater his sister knitted
Snub-nose .38 (Colt Detective Special), 5 rounds loaded, in a clip under the dashboard
Tire iron, under the driver's seat
Car: 1935 Ford V8 Fordor sedan in Vine Street Cab livery, black and yellow, 'Miss Ida', which he owns outright and the cab company only thinks it does
Hack license with his picture on it, City of Kansas City
City street guide, thumbed soft, with the one-way streets inked in
Tank of gasoline (in the trunk, in a can, against emergencies)
features: Knows the Block (City-Born origin: Kansas City, all of it; advantage on Streetwise checks to find a person, place or service in the city; once per foot chase, the GM gives his pursuer the next complication)

Behind the Wheel (Wheelman: advantage on Driving checks in chases and to avoid crashing. In Miss Ida: +15 hit points to the car, his proficiency bonus to its AC while he drives, and once per long rest it drops to 1 instead of 0 and keeps running; he repairs her on a short rest with no check)
Smooth Ride (Wheelman: passengers have no disadvantage firing from the moving car, and advantage on saves in a crash or ram)

Lead Foot (Wheelman, 2nd level: a bonus action each turn to Dash, Disengage or Hide on foot, or, driving, an extra maneuver: sharp turn, sudden stop, or putting the car between his passengers and the shooting)
Style: Getaway Man (Wheelman, 3rd level: as the quarry in a chase he escapes with a lead of 2 rounds instead of 3, and he always knows two ways out of any neighborhood)

Nobody Looks at the Cabbie (Cab Driver background: doormen and other cabbies tell him who went where; in his cab he is scenery and can wait outside anywhere for hours unremarked, and fares say things in the back seat they wouldn't say to a priest)

personality.traits: I talk the whole ride and listen to everything said in the back seat. I know the name of every doorman in the city and the birthday of every cab dispatcher. I whistle the last song I heard until somebody makes me stop.
personality.ideals: A man ought to own the thing he works with. I own Miss Ida. Nobody is ever going to own me.
personality.bonds: My sister Ruthie and her two boys, who live on my fares, and the Vine Street Cab stand, where I have the second-best spot on the street.
personality.flaws: On Sunday morning at ten past four I was parked across from the Gold Leaf with my engine running, and I watched two white men with a badge put Jules Ransom in the back of a green Ford, and I sat there with my hands on the wheel and did not move, because I know what happens to a colored man who follows a police car. I wrote down three numbers of the plate. That's all I did.

appearance: A lean, quick, dark-skinned man of thirty-one with a narrow clever face, a thin moustache, a gap between his front teeth that shows when he grins, which is often, and long restless fingers that drum on whatever is nearest. Cabbie's cap pushed back, horsehide jacket, a pencil behind one ear.
backstory: Cleveland Marchbanks was born on Woodland Avenue in 1905, the fourth of seven children, and named after a president his father admired for reasons nobody can now remember. He left school at fourteen to wash cars at a garage on the Westside, where the Mexican mechanics taught him engines and Spanish, and by twenty he could take a Model T apart and put it back together in the dark. He ran liquor for two years during Prohibition, like half the young men in the city, and got out after a friend was shot on the Blue River road, and in 1930 he bought his first cab on time from a Black-owned company on Vine. He has driven Kansas City for six years, every street of it, and he knows that there are neighbourhoods where his cab is welcome and neighbourhoods where it is stopped and searched, and he knows exactly where the line runs on every block. He has driven Jules Ransom home from the Gold Leaf two nights a week for three years. On Sunday morning Jules waved him off and said he had his own car tonight. Cleve was still sitting there when the Ford came. He has not slept right since.
